newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda trial witness stands by testimony.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda trial witness stands by testimony.

text.p: A Rwandan Tutsi woman witness at the U.N. Rwanda war crimes tribunal, under cross-examination by a Hutu defendant, repeated on Tuesday her testimony that she watched him order the killing of Tutsis.
The woman, known only as "Witness K" to protect her identity, ended nearly nine hours of testimony on Monday and Tuesday against Jean-Paul Akayesu, the former mayor of Rwanda's central Taba commune.

Akayesu, 43, has pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity linked to the mass salughter of 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994. If convicted he faces life imprisonment, the tribunal's highest penalty.

In Rwanda, where separate genocide trials reopened on Tuesday with prominent former politician and businessman Froduald Karamira in the dock, defendants face the death penalty by firing squad if convicted.
Akayesu began cross-examining Witness K on Monday. She stood firm on her testimony made on Friday that she watched him order eight Tutsis hacked to death in front of his office.
"Madam do you confirm that you saw or heard Akayesu give orders to whomsoever it might be to kill persons" from a nearby commune, Akayesu asked.
"I saw that and I heard that," Witness K replied.
"Were these people killed simply because they were Tutsis?" Akayesu asked. "Yes," she responded firmly.
The witness, an accountant at the commune, told the court on Friday how Akayesu had used his authority as mayor to order the slaughter of Tutsis in his commune during the 1994 genocide.
She said Akayesu imprisoned her and threatened to kill her unless she provided information about the whereabouts of other Tutsis.

Presiding Judge Laity Kama of Senegal on Monday granted Akayesu's request to conduct cross-examination himself under tribunal rules setting up a direct confrontation between the accused and his former employee.
Akayesu said on Friday that he wanted to dismiss his lawyers for the third time. The court will rule on the request on Friday.
The prosecution will introduce its second witness during Tuesday's afternoon session, judge Kama said.
Closing the morning session, Swedish judge Lennart Aspegren thanked Witness K and asked if she wanted to say anything further.
"There were many people who were killed in the commune... and this is all due to the acts of Akayesu," she said.

Akayesu is the first suspect to be tried before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda set up to bring to justice the architects of the genocide sparked off by the assassination of Hutu president and military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana in April 1994.

Hutu mobs, militias and soldiers hunted down Tutsis and moderate Hutus opposed to Habyarimana's junta for three months. The mass killings ended only when Tutsi rebels took power and drove the Hutu army into exile in Tanzania, Kenya and Zaire.
